slice: Servers borrow, voters balk, orbit beckons, hackers sprint. Who checks the honesty box?

fewer parking violations once New York pulled UN diplomats' plates

stories.title: Martin Wolf: AI buildout at 3.6% of US GDP raises the risk of a bust
points: Martin Wolf draws on a new Brookings paper by Columbia's Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, which projects US spending on the AI buildout at 3.6% of GDP a year to 2032, a bigger sector boom than the railways of the late 1800s.

Big Tech's spending is now outrunning its cash flow, he notes, so data-centre developers, infrastructure funds and private credit are filling the gap, much of it through loans outsiders can barely see.
His bigger worry is stocks: US valuations sit where they have historically come before crashes, and the longer the boom and the financial engineering run, the harder the landing.
numbers: of US GDP a year on the AI buildout, 2025-32
stories.why: When one theme props up growth, profits and share prices at once, a stall hits jobs, lenders and portfolios together, including Indians who hold US tech through global funds.
stories.other: Booms that end in busts often leave useful infrastructure behind, and if AI profits arrive fast enough today's spending will look prudent. Wolf himself grants AI may still prove transformative.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: the US AI buildout is projected at 3.6% of GDP a year to 2032, financed increasingly by opaque lending, with stock valuations near historic crash levels.
stories.emailHead: Is the AI boom a bubble?
stories.emailTeaser: Martin Wolf weighs what an AI bust would cost

stories.title: AI is speeding up hacks. Are banks in India and abroad ready?
points: An ET Prime analysis notes that India's CERT-In, in an October 15 advisory, saw attackers using AI agents go from first access to impact within hours, exploiting familiar gaps such as exposed credentials and excessive permissions.
It argues bank boards should judge how fast they can spot and shut a breach, and tightly limit what fintech and payment partners can instruct.
In the FT, Chicago Booth's Anil Kashyap calls the Binance hack a warning shot: an AI-aided breach of a major bank is a matter of when, and lightly overseen crypto could be the weak link.
numbers: from first access to impact, per CERT-In
stories.why: As UPI, fintech apps and payment partners plug into banks, a lender's real defence is its slowest link and its slowest decision. That is invisible on a balance sheet, so depositors and shareholders rely on what banks choose to disclose.
stories.other: Banks are among the most watched and best-guarded firms, and AI strengthens defenders too. Years of warnings have passed without a crippling bank breach, so 'when, not if' may overstate the near-term odds.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: CERT-In says AI-agent attacks moved from access to impact within hours; banks are urged to speed up response and limit partner access.
stories.src: The Economic Times and Financial Times
stories.emailTeaser: Attacks now take hours; are bank defences that quick?

stories.title: After a blue wave, data centre fans look to space
points: Democrats won widely on Tuesday, taking the US House and Senate and doing well in Texas, a data-centre hot spot, with many winners campaigning against the industry, Wired reports.
Elon Musk, who spent more than $400 million backing Republicans who all lost, posted that data centres in space now look appealing; investors, researchers and fans joined the chorus.
Experts told Wired change in Texas may be limited: Republicans still hold the state senate, developers' permits carry strong vested rights, and counties lack zoning power over data centres.
numbers: Musk spent on Republicans who lost
stories.why: Local anger over power, water and land has become a vote-winner, and it will shape where AI capacity gets built. Indian states courting data centres should note that welcome can turn quickly.
stories.other: Orbit is no quick escape: Wired notes space data centres cost far more, cannot reach hyperscale size and depend on launches. With a split Texas legislature, change may be slower than either side expects.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: after Democratic wins, tech voices pitched space data centres; Musk spent more than $400 million on losing Republicans, but Texas change faces limits.
stories.emailHead: Data centres eye orbit after vote
stories.emailTeaser: Voters sour on server farms; tech fans look skyward

stories.title: Tim Harford on what stolen sweets and parking fines say about cheats
points: Tim Harford cheers this year's Ig Nobel economics winners, who found upper-class people more likely to take sweets from children, and says the spoof prize shows what makes economists tick.

He recalls classic cheating studies: a bagel seller's honesty box paid best in small offices with well-liked bosses, and UN diplomats' unpaid parking tickets tracked corruption at home until New York pulled plates and violations fell 95%.
His darkest example is a 2012 paper on signing forms honestly, retracted after data sleuths flagged manipulated data; both researchers who supervised the questioned studies deny wrongdoing.
numbers: drop in UN diplomats' parking violations
stories.why: Honour systems, from office tea funds to self-assessed tax returns, work better when someone occasionally checks. And if research on honesty can itself be faked, a single striking study deserves caution.
stories.other: Laughing at cheats can hide how rare outright fraud is; most research is honest, and the parking link is a correlation, not proof that any one diplomat or country is dishonest.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: studies of honesty boxes and diplomats' parking tickets show culture and rules both shape cheating; violations fell 95% once enforcement arrived.
stories.emailTeaser: Sweets, bagels and parking tickets measure our honesty

takeaway.line: Spending, hacking and politics are all outrunning the safeguards meant to catch them. The winners will be whoever builds the brakes in time.
